To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
negotiation of meaning is not the only type of interactional adjustment in the language classroom and that learners may negotiate meaning without any apparent communication problems.

negotiation is one of many processes that facilitate SL2 acquisition, and that it is important to distinguish between negotiation and other conversational processes that may also facilitate SL2 acquisition.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the role of negotiation in the L2 classroom.
the nature of interaction in a second language classroom, and the ways in which it facilitates learning.
how learners work together to negotiate meaning and assist each other to trans-act a task, and how this process relates to the acquisition of language.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
negotiation is an important aspect of the interactional adjustments that facilitate SLA, but it is only one aspect.
the incidence of negotiation of meaning in the language classroom is low, but that negotiation of other aspects of meaning, such as interest and encouragement, is very common.
negotiation is not the only way that learners can gain comprehensible input, and that it is not the only means of interactional adjustment that can assist SLA.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
negotiation is a useful tool for the SLA researcher but not a useful measure of classroom interaction.
negotiation of meaning is a valuable classroom resource, but it is not the only valuable classroom resource, and its value should not be exaggerated.

negotiation of meaning is only one of a number of processes which facilitate second language acquisition in classroom settings, and that these processes need to be identified and measured more carefully if their contribution to SLA is to be fully understood.
The main takeaway from our work is that
negotiation is not the only process that facilitates L2 acquisition.
the value of classroom interaction for SLA cannot be determined solely by counting the number of negotiation moves.

the incidence of negotiation of meaning in the language classroom can be overestimated if the criteria used to define negotiation moves do not take into account the learners’ communicative competence and the nature of their interactional goals.
